mcqs.question: What does adding a CheckoutFacade change about the four underlying subsystem classes?
options: It merges them into a single class
It removes their public methods so only the facade can call them
Nothing about the subsystems changes — they keep their full APIs; the facade just adds a simpler entry point in front of them
It converts them from classes into standalone microservices
mcqs.explanation: Facade is additive: it introduces a new simplified entry point without touching the subsystem classes, which keep working exactly as before for callers who need direct access. It doesn't merge, hide, or restructure the subsystems themselves.

mcqs.question: A CheckoutFacade has grown its own discount calculation and fraud-check logic instead of delegating to a PricingService and FraudService. What's the problem?
options: The facade has taken on business logic that should live in dedicated subsystem classes, turning a thin coordination layer into an unstructured god class
Facades are not allowed to call more than two subsystems
This is correct usage — a Facade is meant to own all business rules for its flow
The facade pattern requires all logic to be stateless
mcqs.explanation: Facade's role is coordination and simplification, not owning domain logic. Letting business rules accumulate in the facade duplicates or shadows what belongs in dedicated services and turns a thin layer into a hard-to-maintain god class. There's no call-count limit, and this is explicitly the wrong pattern for owning business rules.

mcqs.question: A payments team needs to swap Stripe for Adyen behind one interface their app already calls. Which pattern fits best, and why is Facade the wrong lens here?
options: Facade, because it's the general-purpose 'wrap something' pattern
Adapter, because the problem is one interface (the app's PaymentProcessor) not matching another (the new provider's SDK), not simplifying several existing subsystems
Mediator, because payment providers need to coordinate with each other
None of these patterns apply to swapping a payment provider
mcqs.explanation: This is a single mismatched interface, which is Adapter's exact use case — not a case of simplifying access to multiple existing subsystems (Facade) or coordinating peer objects that reference each other (Mediator). Picking the pattern by problem shape, not vague 'wrapping' similarity, is the actual skill being tested.

mcqs.question: A team's internal deployment client hides build, registry-push, and orchestration calls behind one deployService() method, but product teams keep filing requests for custom retry and rollback control per step. What does this suggest?
options: The facade needs more subsystems added to it
The team should rename the facade to a manager class
This is expected and requires no change
Callers need fine-grained control the facade hides — exposing the subsystems directly (or alongside the facade) fits better than forcing everything through one simplified method
mcqs.explanation: Facade trades control for simplicity; when real callers consistently need the control back, that's the pattern's known limit, not a bug to patch by adding more surface to the facade or renaming it. The fix is giving those callers subsystem-level access.
